big_idea: People's core belief about whether abilities are fixed or can be developed, their mindset, shapes how they respond to challenge and failure. A growth mindset tends to produce more resilience, learning, and long-run achievement than a fixed mindset.

tool.label: Fixed mindset vs. growth mindset
tool.text: In a fixed mindset, people believe intelligence is a static trait, so they avoid challenges that risk exposing inadequacy and treat effort itself as a sign of low ability. In a growth mindset, people believe abilities can be developed through effort and better strategies, so setbacks become information rather than a verdict on their worth.
tool.note: Dweck illustrates the framework across sports, business, such as Enron's talent-obsessed culture, and parenting, showing how praising ability versus effort shapes a child's mindset.

ideas.title: Praise the process, not the person
ideas.text: Praising ability tends to instill a fixed mindset in children, while praising effort and strategy supports a growth mindset.

ideas.title: Failure as data, not identity
ideas.text: In a growth mindset, a setback is information about what to try next, not evidence about your fundamental worth.

ideas.title: The talent myth in organizations
ideas.text: Companies that obsess over identifying and rewarding innate talent over developed skill can foster brittle cultures that hide problems instead of solving them.

ideas.title: Mindset in relationships
ideas.text: Fixed-mindset partners expect relationships to just work naturally if they're right for each other; growth-minded partners treat relationship skills as things to build together.

ideas.title: Redefining success
ideas.text: Fixed-mindset success is about proving yourself; growth-mindset success is about stretching your abilities and learning, regardless of the immediate outcome.

ideas.title: Mindsets are learnable
ideas.text: Mindset itself isn't fixed; people can shift from fixed to more growth-oriented thinking with awareness and practice.

try_it: Catch yourself using fixed-mindset language this week, like I'm just not a math person, and reframe it as I haven't learned this yet.
After your next setback, write down one concrete lesson or strategy adjustment instead of a judgment about your ability.
If you mentor someone, practice praising their effort or strategy on a specific task rather than praising them as smart or talented.
Pick one skill you've avoided because you weren't good at it and spend 20 minutes practicing it with a beginner's mindset.
